title: How to Get Bad Smell Out of Shoes

seo.title: How to Get Bad Smell Out of Shoes
seo.meta_description: Get odor out of shoes by addressing moisture first: drying, cleaning, insoles, socks, and when persistent odor may point to sweaty feet or athlete's foot.
seo.search_intent: Remove shoe odor and keep it from returning by addressing the source of moisture.

excerpt: Shoe odor usually comes back when the inside is only perfumed. The more durable fix is to break the moisture cycle: dry the shoes fully, clean what the material allows, and reduce the sweat that keeps re-wetting them.
content_html:
If a pair of shoes smells bad again soon after you put it on, the answer usually is not more fragrance. Odor thrives when sweat and moisture remain trapped inside long enough for odor-producing microbes to build up. A lasting fix starts with drying.

Let the shoes dry all the way through

Remove the insoles if they come out, loosen the laces and tongue, and leave the shoes open in a ventilated place. Do not put the same pair back on while the lining or foam still feels damp. Rotating between pairs gives trapped moisture time to escape.

Avoid blasting shoes with high heat unless the manufacturer says it is safe. Direct heat can distort foam, loosen adhesives, and damage leather or synthetic uppers.

Clean for the material you actually have

If the care label allows machine washing, follow it. For footwear that should not be soaked, wipe the interior with a lightly damp cloth and a small amount of mild detergent, then remove residue. Wash removable insoles separately only if their care instructions allow it, and reinstall them when fully dry.

Do not mix bleach, ammonia, disinfectants, or multiple cleaners inside a shoe. Besides damaging materials, incompatible cleaners can create hazardous fumes.

Baking soda can help, but it is not the whole solution

A small amount of baking soda can absorb some odor and moisture in compatible footwear. Use it dry, let it sit, and shake or vacuum it out thoroughly before wearing. If the shoe stays damp day after day, powder only hides the underlying problem.

Look at socks and feet too

A clean shoe will smell again if it is repeatedly soaked with sweat. Change damp socks and choose fabrics designed to move moisture away from skin. Wash feet and dry carefully between the toes.

The U.K. National Health Service notes that smelly feet are commonly linked to sweat and bacteria and recommends letting shoes dry before wearing them again. The American Academy of Dermatology similarly recommends rotating footwear when sweaty feet are an issue.

When the problem may not be the shoe

Itching, peeling, cracking between the toes, or odor that persists despite good drying can point to a fungal problem such as athlete's foot. In that situation, endlessly deodorizing the shoe misses the source. A pharmacist or health professional can help you choose appropriate treatment.

A routine that is easier to maintain

Open shoes up after wearing them, change wet socks, clean removable insoles when appropriate, and never put damp footwear into a closed closet. If you own two everyday pairs, alternating them often does more than adding stronger fragrance.

If odor returns quickly, look for moisture first. The goal is not to make the shoe smell like something else; it is to keep it from staying damp for hours.

faq.question: Does baking soda remove shoe odor?
faq.answer: It can absorb some odor and moisture, but it works best as a supplement to drying and cleaning.

faq.question: Can shoes go in the washing machine?
faq.answer: Only when the manufacturer or care label allows it; some materials and adhesives can be damaged by soaking.

faq.question: Why does the smell come back so fast?
faq.answer: The shoes may not be drying fully, or they may be getting saturated with sweat again each day.
